---
title: "Finding abbreviations without trusting capitals"
subtitle: "Compare all-capital tokens with parenthetical definitions"
description: "Learn why capital letters create false abbreviation hits and how parenthetical long-form rules behave on constructed examples."
categories: [phrases and entities, abbreviations, workforce research]
---

The Riverton Workforce Lab needs links between short forms and their long
forms. One simple rule finds all-capital tokens as possible abbreviations.

The flyer shows a limitation of that rule.
Its capitalized headings reflect formatting, not necessarily abbreviated
meanings.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created the fictional Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and
its training flyer for teaching.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

In this lesson, you will practice how to:

- find all-capital tokens with a regular expression.
- examine capitalised heading matches.
- measure what a dictionary-and-length guard removes.
- find `Long Form (SHORT)` definitions.
- separate real data from constructed examples.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Find all-capital tokens

The setup reads the text file, expands regex matches, and compares words with
hunspell's dictionary. The stringr package uses the ICU regex engine.
The `[A-Z]` range nevertheless covers only ASCII capitals.
It will not match a token such as `ÉCOLE`.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(hunspell)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

all_caps_pattern <- "\\b[A-Z]{2,}\\b"
all_caps_hits <- sentences |>
  transmute(
    sentence_id,
    text,
    token = str_extract_all(text, all_caps_pattern)
  ) |>
  unnest(token)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  all_caps_hits,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Text", "All-capital token"),
  caption = "All-capital tokens found in the Riverton text",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(all(
  c("readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "tidyr", "purrr", "stringr", "hunspell") %in%
    loadedNamespaces()
))

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(nrow(all_caps_hits), 7L),
  identical(
    all_caps_hits$token,
    c("RIVERTON", "SKILLS", "OPEN", "HOUSE", "DATA", "SUPPORT", "CERTIFICATE")
  ),
  identical(unique(all_caps_hits$sentence_id), c("s023", "s024"))
)
```

An **abbreviation** is a shortened written form, such as `Dr.` or `approx.`.
An **initialism** uses initial letters pronounced separately, as in `NLP`.
An **acronym** uses initial letters pronounced as a word, as in `NATO`.
This rule detects none of those categories directly.
It finds sequences of two or more ASCII capitals, which sometimes correspond
to abbreviations.

Here it finds 7 tokens from `RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE` and
`DATA SUPPORT CERTIFICATE`. Neither heading contains a genuine short-form
abbreviation.

## Score and guard the capital rule

The lesson author examined every all-capital hit in the Riverton text and
found no short-form abbreviations. The guard below keeps only tokens that
are five characters or shorter and absent from the dictionary.

```{r}
scored_caps <- all_caps_hits |>
  mutate(
    true_abbreviation = FALSE,
    token_lower = str_to_lower(token),
    in_dictionary = hunspell_check(token_lower),
    longer_than_five = str_length(token) > 5L,
    guarded_match = !longer_than_five & !in_dictionary,
    removal_reason = case_when(
      in_dictionary & longer_than_five ~ "dictionary word; longer than five",
      in_dictionary ~ "dictionary word",
      longer_than_five ~ "longer than five",
      TRUE ~ "kept"
    )
  )

capital_score <- tibble(
  rule = c("all-capital token", "short and not in dictionary"),
  candidates = c(nrow(scored_caps), sum(scored_caps$guarded_match)),
  hand_rejected = c(
    sum(!scored_caps$true_abbreviation),
    sum(scored_caps$guarded_match & !scored_caps$true_abbreviation)
  ),
  true_abbreviations_found = c(
    sum(scored_caps$true_abbreviation),
    sum(scored_caps$guarded_match & scored_caps$true_abbreviation)
  )
)

guard_details <- scored_caps |>
  select(sentence_id, token, in_dictionary, longer_than_five, guarded_match, removal_reason)

guard_failure_examples <- tibble(token = c("UNESCO", "IT")) |>
  mutate(
    token_lower = str_to_lower(token),
    in_dictionary = hunspell_check(token_lower),
    longer_than_five = str_length(token) > 5L,
    guarded_match = !longer_than_five & !in_dictionary
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  capital_score,
  col.names = c("Rule", "Candidates kept", "Hand-rejected hits", "True abbreviations found"),
  caption = "Human checks of the capital-letter abbreviation rule before and after a filter",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  guard_details,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Token", "In dictionary", "Longer than five", "Kept by guard", "Removal reason"),
  caption = "Dictionary guard details for the all-capital tokens",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  guard_failure_examples,
  col.names = c("Token", "Lowercase token", "In dictionary", "Longer than five", "Kept by guard"),
  caption = "Two real short forms the guard would reject",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(capital_score$candidates, c(7L, 0L)),
  identical(capital_score$hand_rejected, c(7L, 0L)),
  identical(capital_score$true_abbreviations_found, c(0L, 0L)),
  identical(sum(scored_caps$in_dictionary), 6L),
  identical(sum(scored_caps$longer_than_five), 4L),
  identical(any(scored_caps$guarded_match), FALSE),
  identical(scored_caps$in_dictionary[scored_caps$token == "RIVERTON"], FALSE),
  identical(scored_caps$longer_than_five[scored_caps$token == "RIVERTON"], TRUE),
  identical(guard_failure_examples$guarded_match, c(FALSE, FALSE))
)
```

The guard keeps zero candidates. It removes 7 hand-rejected heading words and
finds 0 abbreviations. Removing every match does not establish a good
filter. Six tokens are dictionary words, and four exceed five characters.
Only the length limit removes `RIVERTON`.

The guard also rejects `UNESCO` because of its length.
It rejects `IT` because the dictionary contains `it`.
Results depend on the hunspell dictionary available at execution time.

## Find parenthetical definitions

The Riverton text has no `Long Form (SHORT)` examples.
This section uses a short author-created passage solely to demonstrate the
pattern.

In the code, `\(match_table, current_sentence_id)` is R shorthand for a small
function that handles one sentence's match table and ID.

```{r}
definition_pattern <- regex(
  "\\b((?:[A-Z][a-z]+\\s+){1,}[A-Z][a-z]+)\\s*\\(([A-Z]{2,})\\)"
)

extract_definitions <- function(text, sentence_id) {
  match_tables <- str_match_all(text, definition_pattern)
  pieces <- map2(match_tables, sentence_id, \(match_table, current_sentence_id) {
    if (nrow(match_table) == 0L) {
      return(tibble(
        sentence_id = character(),
        long_form = character(),
        short_form = character()
      ))
    }
    tibble(
      sentence_id = current_sentence_id,
      long_form = str_squish(match_table[, 2]),
      short_form = match_table[, 3]
    )
  })
  list_rbind(pieces)
}

riverton_definitions <- extract_definitions(sentences$text, sentences$sentence_id)
riverton_parenthetical_score <- tibble(
  source = "Riverton text",
  definitions_found = nrow(riverton_definitions)
)

constructed_passage <- tibble(
  sentence_id = c("c001", "c002"),
  text = c(
    "The note defines Natural Language Processing (NLP) for the workshop.",
    "The class lists a Data Support Certificate (DSC) for applicants."
  )
)

definitions <- extract_definitions(
  constructed_passage$text,
  constructed_passage$sentence_id
)

shape_only_example <- extract_definitions(
  "Riverton Skills Centre (NLP)",
  "c003"
)

parenthetical_score <- tibble(
  true_definitions_in_constructed_passage = 2L,
  definitions_found = nrow(definitions)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  riverton_parenthetical_score,
  col.names = c("Source", "Definitions found"),
  caption = "Parenthetical definition rule on the Riverton text",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  definitions,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Long form", "Short form"),
  caption = "Constructed parenthetical abbreviation definitions",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  parenthetical_score,
  col.names = c("True definitions in constructed passage", "Definitions found"),
  caption = "Parenthetical rule on the constructed positive cases",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(riverton_definitions), 0L),
  identical(riverton_parenthetical_score$definitions_found, 0L),
  identical(nrow(definitions), 2L),
  identical(definitions$long_form, c("Natural Language Processing", "Data Support Certificate")),
  identical(definitions$short_form, c("NLP", "DSC")),
  identical(parenthetical_score$definitions_found, 2L),
  identical(shape_only_example$long_form, "Riverton Skills Centre"),
  identical(shape_only_example$short_form, "NLP")
)
```

The parenthetical pattern finds zero Riverton definitions.
It finds `Natural Language Processing (NLP)` and
`Data Support Certificate (DSC)` in the constructed passage.
That passage contains only positive cases.
The result cannot measure false matches or missed definitions.

The pattern matches capitalised words followed by parenthesized capitals.
It does not compare the short-form letters with the long form.
Thus `Riverton Skills Centre (NLP)` also matches.
The Schwartz and Hearst algorithm listed under Sources examines those letter
links and accepts lowercase long forms. This lesson's rule performs fewer
checks.

## What to remember

- All-capital text is only a rough short-form signal.
- The 7 capital-letter hits in the Riverton headings contain 0 abbreviations.
- Keeping 0 of 7 matches does not establish that the guard preserves abbreviations.
- The parenthetical rule finds 2 constructed positive cases and 0 Riverton definitions.
- Parenthetical shape rules need an additional check of short-form letters
  against the long form.

Reject the all-capital rule for these flyer headings.
For future text, retain candidate short forms during rule evaluation.
Evaluate both examples and counter-examples before accepting the rule.
